It provides transparency into the software supply chain, enabling organizations to track, manage, and secure their software assets. SBOMs help in identifying vulnerabilities, ensuring compliance, and mitigating risks associated with third-party and open-source components. ==Importance of SBOM in Software Security and Compliance== SBOMs play a critical role in software security by helping organizations identify and address vulnerabilities before they can be exploited. They enhance compliance with industry regulations and standards by ensuring that organizations can verify software integrity, track software origins, and detect unauthorized modifications. SBOMs also improve risk management by providing visibility into potential security threats within the software supply chain. ==Key Components of an SBOM== The SBOM includes at minimum the baseline attributes defined by [US-NTIA SBOM]. These baseline attributes are: * Author Name * Timestamp * Supplier Name * Component Name * Version String * Component HASH * Unique Identifier * Relationship [[File:sbom baseline attributes example.png|thumb|center|500px|Baseline SBOM Example]] =SBOM Generation= ==Methods for Generating SBOMs== SBOMs can be generated using various tools, each designed for different environments and programming languages. The SBOM has to be generated in both machine-readable formats (e.g., CycloneDX, SPDX) and human-readable formats (e.g., spreadsheet). '''CDXGEN''', a polyglot '''CycloneDX''' SBOM generator, is highly recommended as it supports multiple languages and platforms, making it versatile for diverse ecosystems. ==Examples - SBOM Generation & Vulnerability Scanning Tools & Programming Languages== The following table lists example projects and the tools / commands used to generate a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), categorized by programming language. The table can be expanded at any time to include additional projects, languages, or tools. {| class="wikitable" ! Supported Build Tools ! Link to Supported Build Tools ! Supported SBOM Standards ! Supported Languages !Project |- | * SBOM Generation: '''Gradle''' * Vulnerability Scanning: n.a. | [https://github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-gradle-plugin CycloneDX Gradle Plugin] | CycloneDX v1.6 | Java |ELARA |- | * SBOM Generation:'''Gradle''' * Vulnerability Scanning: n.a. | [https://github.com/spdx/spdx-gradle-plugin SPDX Gradle Plugin] | SPDX v2.3 | Java |ELARA |- | * SBOM Generation: '''CMake''' * Vulnerability Scanning: n.a. | [https://github.com/microsoft/sbom-tool Microsoft SBOM Tool] | SPDX v3.0 | C/C++ |ELARA |- | * SBOM Generation: '''Yocto''' * Vulnerability Scanning: '''Yocto''' | [https://docs.yoctoproject.org/dev/dev-manual/sbom.html Yocto Project SBOM] | SPDX v2.3, CVE | Various (Prebuilt Linux Packages) |ELARA |- | * SBOM Generation: '''CycloneDX''' * Vulnerability Scanning: '''bomber''' | *[https://github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-buildroot CycloneDX Buildroot] *[https://devops-kung-fu.github.io/bomber bomber] |CycloneDX v1.6 |Linux Packages supported by Buildroot |Metis |- | * SBOM Generation: '''CycloneDX''' * Vulnerability Scanning: '''bomber''' | *[https://github.com/CycloneDX/cyclonedx-node-npm cyclonedx-node-npm] *[https://devops-kung-fu.github.io/bomber bomber] |CycloneDX v1.6 |node.js packages |Metis |- | * SBOM Generation: created out of image manually with '''Syft''' * Vulnerability Scanning: '''Grype''' | * [https://github.com/anchore/syft Syft] * [https://github.com/anchore/grype Grype] (REFRACTOR Files: [[:File:Vulnerability_Analysis.pdf|Documentation Vulnerability Analysis Process]] Outcome: L:\Daten_FE\1_PRODUKTE\7_Phoropter\00_Wild\02_Software\01_Security\01_Vulnerability_Analysis\R1.02) | SPDX, CVE | linux image (details see description of tool grype) |Refractor 900 |} = SBOM Vulnerability Scanning = == Methodology == Finding vulnerabilities with a scanning tool is the first step. The SBOM is scanned, and the components compared to information from vulnerability databases to obtain a list of vulnerable components and their vulnerabilities. See for example https://sbom-cve-check.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction.html Next we need a process to analyse them and decide what to do with them, using the available human effort in the most efficient way while keeping a high precision. This is the main topic of this guide To do this, gather additional information, then apply the CISA Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC) Guidehttps://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/cisa-ssvc-guide%20508c.pdf to decide what actions to take. We gather information from: * CVE and OVD databases to gather technical information about detected vulnerabilities (CVSS Vector) * CISA data and list of known exploited vulnerabilities gives us information that we use in the SVCC methodology to determine the security risk and decision taking * When CISA data is not available, and CVSS contains the necessary optional data, we convert the CVSS data to SVCC (See tables below) * We compare EPSS (exploitation probability model) and CISA (list of exploited vulnerabilities) and keep the highest SVCC exploitability factor. ==Desicion Tree== The CISA '''Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC)''' is a model that uses '''decision trees''' to help different organizations and individuals (stakeholders) prioritize their response to vulnerabilities. Unlike traditional scoring systems like CVSS, SSVC aims to provide '''qualitative action decisions''' rather than just a numerical score. [[File:ssvc_desicions.jpg]] {| class="wikitable sortable" ! Category ! Option(s) ! Explanation |- | Exploitation | None | No known exploitation or activity. The vulnerability is theoretical or mitigated. |- | Exploitation | PoC (Proof of Concept) | Exploitation has been demonstrated in a controlled or research setting but not seen in the wild. |- | Exploitation | Active | Exploitation has been observed in real-world attacks or within the environment. |- | Automatable | Yes | The vulnerability can be exploited or scanned automatically (e.g., via scripts or tools). |- | Automatable | No | Manual steps or human expertise are required for exploitation. |- | Technical Impact | Partial | The vulnerability affects a subset of systems, data, or functionality; limited technical control gained. |- | Technical Impact | Total | Full compromise of system, data, or privileges is possible (e.g., root/admin access). |- | Mission & Well-being Impact | Low | Minimal effect on mission success, operations, or safety. |- | Mission & Well-being Impact | Medium | Noticeable degradation in mission performance or user well-being. |- | Mission & Well-being Impact | High | Severe impact—mission failure, loss of critical data, or significant harm to well-being. |} In our company we use the following decision outcomes and its corresponding actions as shown in table below: {| class="wikitable" ! style="text-align:center;" | Decision ! style="text-align:center;" | Action ! style="text-align:center;" | Corresponding Risk Level |- | style="background:#ff0000;" | '''Act''' | style="background:#ff0000;" | Requires urgent corrective action | style="background:#ff0000;" | High / Critical |- | style="background:#ffff00;" | '''Attend''' | style="background:#ffff00;" | Requires corrective action in the next regular release / Change Order | style="background:#ffff00;" | Medium |- | style="background:#00ff00;" | '''Track''' | style="background:#00ff00;" | Does not require action at the current time | style="background:#00ff00;" | Low |} ==Automation== This decision process can be automated using a script that retrieves the relevant '''SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization)''' values for a given '''CVE''' (e.g., from https://cve.org):
[[File:ssvc-values.jpg|450px]] For simplicity, the script assumes the '''highest Mission and Well-being impact value (High)''' by default. It then generates a '''decision table''' containing the possible outcomes — '''Track''', '''Attend''', and '''Act''' — for each vulnerability. The resulting table can be '''filtered''' to highlight only vulnerabilities with '''Attend''' or '''Act''' outcomes, providing an initial prioritization. Subsequently, all vulnerabilities marked as '''Act''' or '''Attend''' should undergo '''manual assessment''' to further refine and validate the prioritization results. If '''no SSVC values''' are available, the following tables define the '''conversion criteria''' for mapping '''CVSS metrics''' to their corresponding '''SSVC values''', as illustrated below: {| class="wikitable" |+ Conversion from CVSS v3 to SSVC |- ! SSVC !! Conversion rule !! Notes |- | Exploitation.active || if CVSS exploit code maturity is "high" or "functional exploit exists", or if EPSS score is >= 10% || - |- | Exploitation.poc || if CVSS exploit code maturity is "proof of concept available", or if 5% < EPSS score < 10% || - |- | Exploitation.none || if CVSS exploit code maturity is "Unproven that exploit exists" or if EPSS score < 5% || When the exploit is purely theoretical or no code exists |- | Exploitation.undefined|| if CVSS exploit code maturity is "Not defined" and no EPSS score for this CVE exists || In CVSS, "Exploit code maturity" is optional. |- | Automatable.yes|| if CVSS attack vector is "network" or "adjacent network" and attack complexity is low, and no or low privileges are required, and no user interaction is required || Here we use the CVSS Exploitability metrics (mandatory). "Local" attack vector means that the attack can not be performed over the network, but only using read/write/execute capabilities of the system. In general, such an attack requires user interaction to upload a malicious file, or that the attacker logs into the system to upload the malicious component. We therefore consider it not automatable. |- | Automatable.no|| when the above conditions are not true || It means that the success of an attack relies on parameters outside the attacker's control |- | Technical_impact.total || if '''any''' of the CVSS Impact metrics is "high" || CVSS evaluates Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. SSVC says that impact is "total" when the exploit gives the adversary total control over the behavior of the software, or gives total disclosure of all information on the system that contains the vulnerability. |- | Technical_impact.partial || if '''none''' of the CVSS Impact metrics is "high" || - |- |} {| class="wikitable" |+ Conversion from CVSS v4 to SSVC |- ! SSVC !! Conversion rule !! Notes |- | Exploitation.active || if CVSS exploit maturity is "attacked", or if EPSS score is >= 10% || The selection is made by chosing the highest exploitation value of CVSS or EPSS |- | Exploitation.poc || if CVSS exploit maturity is "proof of concept", or if 5% < EPSS score < 10% || |- | Exploitation.none || if CVSS exploit code maturity is "Unreported" or if EPSS score < 5% || When the exploit is purely theoretical or no code exists |- | Exploitation.undefined|| if CVSS exploit code maturity is "Not defined" and no EPSS score for this CVE exists || In CVSS, "Exploit code maturity" is optional. |- | Automatable.yes|| if CVSS automatable is yes (optional field) or if CVSS attack vector is "network" or "adjacent network" and attack complexity is low, and no or low privileges are required, and no or passive user interaction is required || Here we use the CVSS Exploitability metrics (mandatory). "Local" attack vector means that the attack can not be performed over the network, but only using read/write/execute capabilities of the system. In general, such an attack requires user interaction to upload a malicious file, or that the attacker logs into the system to upload the malicious component. We therefore consider it not automatable. |- | Automatable.no|| when the above conditions are not true || It means that the success of an attack relies on parameters outside the attacker's control |- | Technical_impact.total || if '''any''' of the CVSS Impact metrics of either the vulnerable system, or the subsequent system, is "high" || CVSS evaluates Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. SSVC says that impact is "total" when the exploit gives the adversary total control over the behavior of the software, or gives total disclosure of all information on the system that contains the vulnerability. |- | Technical_impact.partial || if '''none''' of the CVSS Impact metrics of either the vulnerable system, or the subsequent system, is "high" || - |- |} ==Python Code For Automation== Gitlab Group for Security Tools: https://git.haag-streit.com/tools/security/ = SBOM Output = The SBOM is documented by using the template [[SBOM - Software Bill of Materials]]. = References =
